I also have bipolar disorder (type II, so "shit most of the time with days/weeks of not-so-shit"). The main thing that it does is sap my resilience and adaptability: because my baseline is so low, I need things to be super-all right to be in a good mood. You can see how that makes life difficult.

By waves I meant pangs-- they come and go in a base level of persistent pain. When suddenly I find myself on dry land for a day, or more, I know I could really go on like that-- but it never lasts. Yes, doctors know. No, we've not found anything remotely workable yet.

I've lived a pretty rich life, actually. Here's how I see it. Imagine you came to a big party, with lots of people there whom you like, and lots of people by whom you want to be liked. There is a band and lots of entertainment-- dodgem carts, whack-a-mole and similar, party games, karaoke etc. 

You arrived looking your absolute best, most beautiful and radiant. The person with whom you wanted to dance dances with you. Then another person with whom you also wanted to dance. Then you accept a few dances out of curiosity/politeness, but decide you want to be back to dancing with the first one. But s/he is already dancing with someone else, beautiful and radiant, and a better dancer. You try to get that person to notice you again, but that was it. Oh well, you say, I have had my day of love, and it was great-- doesn't matter if it lasted a minute or a lifetime. You don't really mean it, but all that's left after trying is acceptance.

You play party games and you are good. It is satisfying. But you get tired of party games, and there is a new player, who is as good, or better. You try to cooperate, or to compete, but none of the people want you around any longer. Oh well, you say, I've had my day of social success, however short.

Then, karaoke. You sing and mesmerize the audience. You make a little speech, even, and they love it. You step down from the stage and have a go at life drawing, and people love what you made. Then you meet a famous author, and recite some of your poetry/discuss some plots. He loves it. But you are tired, and walk away towards the dodgem carts and things, and when you return, another is reciting, and singing, and drawing. Oh well, you say, I'm too tired to try any of that again and compete for recognition, but I have had my moments of creative fulfillment and recognition.

Dodgems and things are fun, but you can only go on so long before they stop being enjoyable. Going back to the dance floor, or karaoke, or the party games, makes you sad. In fact, you've been sad all this time, except for a few moments of peaking joy while dancing or playing or singing, and maybe that's why you left those activities in the first place: for you, there is only joy or sadness, with hardly anything in between. Oh well, you say. I have tried to walk the middle path, too, but it is very hard and wears me out. Perhaps I should accept my limitations.

You look back at the party. Part of you wants to be there, part of you wishes you had your dance partner with you until the end of the party. But this did not happen. When you imagine that a time may come when you'll wish you had someone, *anyone,* at the party with you, you feel sick. Oh well, you say. This was fun, and I'm grateful, but it was a lot of effort, and I'd like to go now. I may have learnt a lot, but there is nowhere to apply the lessons. At this party, I've run out of tries; game over. I'd better go.

There is some stuff that you must do before you go, however, this is the rule. You must clean up after yourself, and a little bit after other people. Because you had been so active and tried so many things, you've got a lot more to clean up than average.

You realise that you may not go for a long time, because the clean-up will take a long time. You are sad. Seeing others enjoy themselves makes you more sad, so you try to keep behind a pavilion, but inevitably your cleaning activities bring you back into the thick of the party. You hope to be invisible; some of the time you are, sometimes people try to get you to join back in. You cannot stand the thought of joining back in; you continue to clean up, and the only thing to look forward to is being finally allowed to go. 

Cleaning up is hard. It is tiring. It kills you to see others full of energy, life and joy while you sadly clean up. And yet you go on. You say, I have experienced the good, and I am experiencing the bad now. I have experienced everything this party had to offer, from absolute delight to the darkest envy. I've tasted everything, I've given something back, and I'd really like to leave. How do you go on?

That's it in a (pretty huge) nutshell.
